_meta.note: N-D-C values derived from published transparency levels, monitoring data coverage, and structural constraints per phase. Balance scores reflect phase-specific transparency tiers adjusted for known accumulation and opacity constraints. Corrective mechanism (TVPCI-R) scored as PROVISIONAL due to absence of phase-resolved global LCA equivalents for plastic remediation.

coherence_scores.e_basis: Financial abstraction coupling: ratio of dedicated plastic remediation funding (estimated $1.5B/yr globally for ocean cleanup operations) to what would be required to match the accumulation rate at current removal efficiency. Score reflects severe structural disconnection between available financial instruments and measurable physical outcomes. No standardized bond KPI framework exists for ocean plastic metrics as of 2026.

synthetic.label: Global Baseline 2024
synthetic.description: Global plastic production and dispersal chain, 2024 reference year. All phases reflect current operational state derived from published monitoring data. Production: approximately 400 Mt/year. Ocean stock: approximately 150-250 Mt accumulated since 1950. Deep-sea sediment: estimated 5.6 Mt in surface sediments alone (Pabortsava and Lampitt 2020).

0.name: Polymer Production
0.transformation: Petroleum and petrochemical feedstocks converted to polymer resins and plastic goods
0.custodian: Petrochemical industry (BASF, Dow, LyondellBasell, Sinopec) and converters

1.name: Product Use and Fragmentation
1.transformation: Plastic goods degrade via UV radiation, mechanical stress, and thermal cycling into macro- and micro-fragments
1.custodian: End consumers, waste management systems, environment (uncontrolled)

2.name: Terrestrial Dispersal
2.transformation: Microplastics distribute through soil, agricultural land, and urban surfaces via wind, runoff, and wastewater
2.custodian: Environment (uncontrolled); agricultural systems; municipal wastewater operators

3.name: Freshwater Transport
3.transformation: Microplastics mobilized by rivers, streams, and groundwater systems toward coastal discharge zones
3.custodian: River systems; water utilities; upstream land management authorities

4.name: Marine Surface Dispersal
4.transformation: Microplastics concentrate in ocean gyres, undergo photodegradation and biofouling, and fractionate by size and density
4.custodian: Ocean circulation systems; GPML/GESAMP monitoring; The Ocean Cleanup operations

5.name: Deep-Sea Sediment Accumulation
5.transformation: Dense and biofouled microplastics settle to the seabed, entering sediment columns over geological timescales

6.name: Biological Uptake
6.transformation: Microplastics ingested and absorbed by filter feeders, fish, plankton, and marine invertebrates
6.custodian: Marine food web; emerging plastisphere microbial communities

7.name: Trophic Transfer and Bioaccumulation
7.transformation: Microplastics and associated chemical additives concentrate through food web trophic levels, reaching apex predators and humans

0.notes: Polymer feedstock conversion to plastic goods. High transparency: production volumes reported by PlasticsEurope, IEA, and UNEP with good coverage. D reflects strict polymer specifications, REACH compliance, safety regulations, and quality constraints that define each resin type. C reflects the massive production output (approximately 400 Mt/year globally in 2023) distributed across packaging (36%), construction, automotive, and electronics. Primary structural tension: high-quality production controls (high D) combined with very limited take-back or end-of-life design accountability (reducing effective C recovery). Recycled content share remains below 10% of global production.
0.key_metric: Global plastic production: ~400 Mt/year (2023); mechanical recycling rate: ~9% globally; incineration: ~19%; landfill/environment: ~72% (Geyer et al. 2017 Science Advances)
0.corrective_mechanisms: Extended producer responsibility (EPR) legislation in EU, UK, Canada; plastic credits markets; design for recyclability standards. Coverage: approximately 35% of global production under some form of EPR by 2024.
0.scope_source: IEA 2023: Plastics and climate — average 1.9 tCO2 scope 1 per tonne polymer produced

1.notes: Plastic goods in use gradually fragment through UV photolysis, mechanical abrasion, thermal stress, and biodegradation to form microplastic particles (<5 mm). D reflects the photodegradation rate constants and mechanical stress thresholds that define when fragmentation occurs and at what rate. C reflects the actual fragmentation output entering the environment: estimated 9.5 Mt/year entering water environments globally (Lebreton and Andrady 2019). Balance is stressed because: (1) fragmentation is largely uncontrolled and occurs wherever plastic is exposed to UV and mechanical forces; (2) collection infrastructure captures a fraction of waste before fragmentation occurs; and (3) littering, illegal dumping, and inadequate collection in low-income regions generate large uncontrolled fragmentation streams. Secondary microplastics (tyre wear, synthetic textiles, fishing gear) account for approximately 35% of ocean microplastic inputs.
1.key_metric: ~9.5 Mt/year enters water environments (Lebreton and Andrady 2019); tyre wear particles: 0.5-1.5 Mt/year; synthetic textile fibres: 0.2-0.5 Mt/year; fishing gear: 0.7 Mt/year (OECD 2022)
1.corrective_mechanisms: Urban stormwater filters; tyre particle filters; synthetic textile wash filters (PlanetCare, Cora Ball); beach cleanup operations (global ~150,000 tonnes/year collected; marginal vs. total input). No viable capture mechanism at fragmentation scale.

2.notes: Terrestrial microplastic dispersal through soil and land surfaces. Terrestrial microplastic concentrations are estimated at 4-23x higher than ocean concentrations by mass (Nizzetto et al. 2016 Environ Sci Technology). D reflects soil retention capacity, plant uptake thresholds, and erosion and runoff dynamics. C reflects the actual monitored stock and flux: agricultural soils receive an estimated 125,000-850,000 tonnes of microplastics annually through biosolid (sewage sludge) application alone. Atmospheric microplastic transport deposits an estimated 1,000-10,000 tonnes/year in remote ecosystems including mountain ranges and Arctic. Opacity is medium-low: monitoring programs exist in Europe (LUCAS soil survey) but global coverage is highly inconsistent. Data quality degrades sharply outside Europe and North America.
2.key_metric: Agricultural soil microplastic from biosolid application: 125,000-850,000 t/year (Nizzetto et al. 2016); atmospheric deposition in Pyrenees: 365 particles/m2/day (Dris et al. 2016 Nat Geosci); Global soil stock: estimated 4-23x ocean surface stock
2.corrective_mechanisms: Biosolid treatment improvements (wastewater microplastic removal: 95-99% in advanced treatment plants, but removed particles concentrate in sludge applied to land); soil remediation technology is nascent and unscalable at current cost.

3.notes: Freshwater systems (rivers, lakes, groundwater) transport microplastics from terrestrial sources to coastal marine environments. D reflects watershed retention capacity, filtration potential through riparian zones and wetlands, and upstream waste management infrastructure constraints. C reflects the measured flux: global river plastic input to oceans estimated at 0.41-4 Mt/year (Lebreton et al. 2017 Nature Comm; Schmidt et al. 2017 Environ Sci Technology). The range reflects substantial data uncertainty. Asian rivers dominate, with the top 10 rivers (primarily in South and Southeast Asia) responsible for approximately 88-95% of river-borne plastic input. The Ocean Cleanup Interceptor system operates in river environments and has removed approximately 1,800 tonnes as of 2024 — approximately 0.04-0.4% of annual input. Balance is stressed: river monitoring exists (microplastic counts per m3 are measurable), but the temporal and spatial variability is high and collection data is poorly standardized globally.
3.key_metric: River plastic input to oceans: 0.41-4 Mt/year (Lebreton et al. 2017); top 10 rivers: 88-95% of total input; Ocean Cleanup Interceptor removal 2019-2024: ~1,800 tonnes
3.corrective_mechanisms: River barriers (Ocean Cleanup Interceptors: 11 deployed globally as of 2024); wastewater treatment microplastic removal (high efficiency but particles concentrate in biosolid sludge); watershed restoration improving retention.

4.notes: Marine surface microplastics concentrate in the five major subtropical gyres through convergent surface currents and Stokes drift. D reflects gyre circulation constraints, biofouling dynamics that alter particle buoyancy, and photodegradation rates that continue to fragment particles. C reflects the monitored surface concentration: Eriksen et al. (2014) estimated 5.25 trillion particles and 268,940 tonnes at the ocean surface. More recent models (Kaandorp et al. 2023) suggest this is a significant underestimate as neutrally buoyant particles in the upper 200 m are not captured by surface trawls. Balance is the lowest of the monitored phases: while significant monitoring programs exist (GPML, Sea Education Association, 5 Gyres Institute), the measurement system captures only the visible surface fraction. Below the thermocline and in deep-sea sediments, the stock is largely unmeasured. The Ocean Cleanup System 03 has removed approximately 3,000 tonnes from the North Pacific Gyre as of 2024.
4.key_metric: Ocean surface particles: 5.25 trillion (Eriksen et al. 2014); surface mass: 268,940 tonnes; North Pacific Gyre concentration: up to 100 g/km2 in accumulation zone; Ocean Cleanup System 03 removal: ~3,000 tonnes (2019-2024)
4.corrective_mechanisms: The Ocean Cleanup surface systems (System 03 operational in North Pacific Gyre); commercial fleet debris interception (marginal); natural photodegradation at surface (converts macro to micro, not removal).

5.notes: Deep-sea sediment accumulation is the largest and most opaque reservoir in the global plastic cycle. Microplastics that biofoul and increase in density sink below the thermocline and settle to the seabed. Pabortsava and Lampitt (2020, Nature Communications) estimated 11-41 million tonnes of microplastics in the upper 200 m of the water column alone, far exceeding previous surface estimates. Sediment core samples from the deep Atlantic show microplastic concentrations of 1.9 particles/10 mL in surface sediments, with some hotspots exceeding 9,000 particles/100 mL near submarine canyon systems. D reflects the physical settling dynamics, benthic current redistribution, and geological burial rates that constrain particle residence time. C reflects the near-zero recovery capacity: no technology exists for deep-sea microplastic remediation at any meaningful scale. This phase is the primary analytical driver of the evolutionary stress prediction: the combination of massive stock, low transparency, and zero corrective capacity creates the strongest D-C divergence in the system.
5.key_metric: Estimated deep water column stock: 11-41 Mt in top 200m (Pabortsava and Lampitt 2020); deep-sea sediment: up to 9,200 particles/100mL in submarine canyon hotspots (Kane et al. 2020 Science); monitoring coverage: <0.1% of deep-sea floor sampled
5.corrective_mechanisms: None at scale. Biological degradation by benthic organisms (sea cucumbers, polychaetes) is documented but operates on timescales of decades to centuries. Bacterial communities in deep-sea plastisphere are emerging (Amobacter, Roseovarius documented on deep-sea plastic). No human remediation technology exists for deep-sea microplastic extraction.

6.notes: Marine organisms from zooplankton to filter feeders to fish actively ingest microplastics, both deliberately (mistaking particles for food) and incidentally (consuming microplastic-contaminated prey). Over 700 species have been documented with microplastic ingestion. D reflects organismal filtration capacity, gut passage rates, the biological threshold at which particles cause physical damage, and the chemical toxicity of plastic additives and adsorbed pollutants. C reflects the biological uptake flux: mussels filter approximately 4.6 microplastic particles per hour; blue whales consume an estimated 10 million microplastic particles per day; deep-diving fish bring surface-concentrated particles to depth. This phase is also where natural biological correction first becomes measurable: plastisphere communities (Ideonella sakaiensis and related organisms) have been documented degrading PET at rates of 0.13 mg/cm2 per day at 30 degrees C. However, this corrective capacity is orders of magnitude below the accumulation rate. Balance at 60.0% is the second-lowest measured phase.
6.key_metric: Species with documented ingestion: >700 (Gall and Thompson 2015 Marine Pollution Bulletin); mussel ingestion rate: ~4.6 particles/hr; global fisheries microplastic ingestion: estimated 100,000 particles per second; Ideonella sakaiensis PET degradation rate: 0.13 mg/cm2/day at 30C (Yoshida et al. 2016)
6.corrective_mechanisms: Natural: plastisphere bacterial communities (Ideonella sakaiensis, Pseudomonas spp., Bacillus subtilis) degrading PET and other polymers at measurable but sub-scale rates. Human: zero direct intervention at biological uptake phase. Indirect: upstream source reduction reduces input rate.

7.notes: Trophic transfer concentrates microplastics and associated chemical additives (phthalates, bisphenols, PFAS, PCBs) through successive trophic levels. Primary mechanisms: biomagnification of plastic-adsorbed persistent organic pollutants (POPs), physical accumulation in gut and tissue, and chemical leaching of endocrine disruptors. Human tissue presence is now confirmed: Leslie et al. (2022) detected microplastics in 17 of 22 human blood samples; Ragusa et al. (2021) detected microplastics in human placenta; lung tissue, colon, and liver presence also documented. D reflects trophic transfer efficiency, metabolic processing capacity, and excretion rates that limit tissue retention. C reflects the documented but contested bioaccumulation: human blood microplastic concentrations are measurable but highly variable (1.6 micrograms per mL in Leslie 2022). This is the lowest-balance phase in the chain (50.5%) and the key evolutionary stress signal: a phase approaching breakdown with no natural or human corrective mechanism operating at scale.
7.key_metric: Human blood microplastics: detected in 17/22 samples at mean 1.6 ug/mL (Leslie et al. 2022); human placenta: 4 tissue types affected (Ragusa et al. 2021); POPs biomagnification factor: up to 1,000,000x from seawater to apex predator tissue (Rochman et al. 2013)
7.corrective_mechanisms: None operational. No technology exists to remove microplastics from living tissue at individual or population scale. Fecal excretion of some particles is documented (Schwabl et al. 2019 Ann Intern Med: 9 particle types in human stool), but tissue retention rate and long-term effects are unknown. Upstream source reduction is the only available lever.

synthetic.interpretation: The global plastic biosphere chain shows a progressive collapse from Coherent production (Phase 0, 89.3%) through Stressed dispersal (Phases 1-4, 68-79%) to Failure accumulation and uptake (Phases 5-7, 51-60%). The structural break occurs at the marine-biological boundary: Phases 0-4 have measurable monitoring data and at least partial human corrective capacity; Phases 5-7 have very low transparency and no corrective mechanism operating at scale relative to the accumulation rate. Phase 7 (Trophic Transfer, 50.5%) is the primary bottleneck and the most critical evolutionary stress signal: it is the deepest in the Failure zone, has the lowest data quality, and has zero available corrective mechanisms at individual or population scale. The chain's average balance of 69.2% (Stressed) is misleading: the productive upper phases (0-4) inflate the average, masking the breakdown trajectory of the lower phases. The tholonic model predicts corrective mechanisms will emerge first and most intensively at Phase 5 (deep-sea sediment) and Phase 6 (biological uptake), where the D-C divergence is largest and the biological evolutionary pressure is most concentrated.
